# `catalog`: summarize point cloud files {#sec-catalog}

## What it does

`catalog` is the first tool to run on a new delivery of lidar data. It
reads every LAS/LAZ file given to it and reports each file's point count,
bounding box, elevation range, LAS point format, and whether it is
compressed. With `/density`, it also writes a raster counting the points
in each cell, which shows at a glance whether coverage is even or has gaps
and stripes.

`catalog` needs no ground surface and changes no data.

## Example commands

{{< include ../examples/fragments/catalog_commands.md >}}

## Options used

| Option | Value | What it does |
|:--------|:--------------------|:-------------------------|
| (input) | `TC_1372_forest200ft.laz` | The file to summarize. A folder summarizes every LAS/LAZ file in it, one row per file. |
| `/output` | `out/catalog/catalog.csv` | The CSV report. |
| `/density` | `10` | Also write a point-count raster with 10 ft cells, named after the report (`catalog.tif`). |

: Options used in the `catalog` example. {#tbl-options-catalog}

## Outputs

- **`catalog.csv`**: one row per input file, with the columns
  `FileName`, `PointCount`, `MinX`, `MaxX`, `MinY`, `MaxY`, `MinZ`,
  `MaxZ`, `Format` (LAS point data format), and `IsCompressed`.
- **`catalog.tif`**: one band, `point_density`, holding the number of
  points in each cell. The grid starts at the data's lower-left corner
  and carries the input's coordinate system.

## Results

@fig-catalog-density maps the density raster. The black outline is the
bounding box from the CSV report; it sits on the edge of the grid, which
confirms the raster is placed on the tile's real coordinates. Counts are
fairly even across the tile. Stripes along one direction would mark
overlapping flight lines, and empty cells inside the tile would point to
missing data.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/catalog_figures.md >}}

## Checks

@tbl-checks-catalog lists the checks on this run. They confirm that the
reported point count and bounding box match the file, and that the
density raster sits on the tile, carries a coordinate system, and counts
every point exactly once.
